course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?
themes.example: Examination preparation favored families that could afford education.

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems
themes.question: How were goods produced, exchanged, taxed, or distributed?
themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions
themes.question: How did beliefs, learning, and artistic practices influence society?
themes.example: Buddhist monasteries connected religious practice with education.

themes.title: Technology and innovation
themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?
themes.example: Inca roads and knotted records helped officials coordinate resources.

questions.prompt: Why was Champa rice important in China?
choices: It ripened quickly, so Chinese farmers stopped irrigating their fields
It grew in deserts, so farming spread into northern China's steppes
It ripened quickly, allowing more than one harvest in some regions
It replaced wheat as the main crop throughout all of northern China
questions.explanation: Fast-ripening rice allowed double cropping in suitable areas of southern China, raising food supplies.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Quick ripening is correct, but rice still depended on irrigation and water management.
Champa rice needed water; it did not make deserts farmable.
Fast-ripening rice allowed double cropping in suitable areas of southern China, raising food supplies.
Rice spread mainly in the wetter south; wheat and millet remained important in the north.
questions.distinguisher: The advantage was speed of ripening in places with enough water.

questions.prompt: How did trade networks contribute to the spread of the bubonic plague?
choices: Merchants, soldiers, and animals moved fleas and rats between regions
Traders deliberately carried the disease in order to weaken rival trading cities
Contaminated silk was the only way the disease could travel
Merchants, soldiers, and animals moved the disease only by sea
questions.explanation: Movement of people, goods, and animals along land and sea routes carried infected fleas and rodents.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Movement of people, goods, and animals along land and sea routes carried infected fleas and rodents.
Plague spread through ordinary movement, not a deliberate trading plan.
Plague was carried by fleas on rodents and in goods, not by silk alone.
Ships spread plague to ports, but it also traveled overland along caravan routes.
questions.distinguisher: Mobility along both land and sea routes.

questions.prompt: How did the Black Death affect labor in parts of western Europe?
choices: Labor demand fell because landlords stopped farming after the plague
Labor shortages let all peasants immediately escape their obligations
Labor surpluses drove wages down because so many workers survived
Labor shortages let some surviving workers demand higher wages
questions.explanation: With so many dead, workers were scarce, and some could bargain for better pay or conditions.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Farming continued, and landlords competed for scarce workers.
Workers gained leverage, but lords and governments resisted with laws limiting wages and movement.
The plague killed a huge share of the population, creating shortages, not surpluses.
With so many dead, workers were scarce, and some could bargain for better pay or conditions.
questions.distinguisher: Fewer workers increased bargaining power, though results varied.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of human activity changing the environment in this period?
choices: Expanding farmland caused monsoon winds to change their seasonal direction
Expanding farmland and grazing led to deforestation in some regions
Trade routes caused the Sahara to turn into grassland after 1300
Silk production in China caused the Black Sea to dry up
questions.explanation: Clearing forests for farms, fuel, and pasture reshaped landscapes across Afro-Eurasia.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Farming changed land and forests, but it did not alter monsoon wind patterns.
Clearing forests for farms, fuel, and pasture reshaped landscapes across Afro-Eurasia.
The Sahara remained desert throughout this period.
The Black Sea did not dry up; this has no basis.
questions.distinguisher: Look for a plausible local change in land use.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where did the plague come from before reaching Florence?
choices: It began among Florence's own merchants after a bad harvest
It appeared in the East years earlier and spread westward
It arrived suddenly from Africa across the Mediterranean
It appeared in Florence first and then spread to the East
questions.explanation: Boccaccio says it “had some years before appeared in the parts of the East” and spread toward the West.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments
First Day, introduction

choiceExplanations: Boccaccio describes the disease arriving from elsewhere, not beginning in Florence.
Boccaccio says it “had some years before appeared in the parts of the East” and spread toward the West.
Boccaccio names the East, not Africa, as the source.
This reverses Boccaccio's account.
questions.distinguisher: Use Boccaccio's own words about direction.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Giovanni Boccaccio, Florentine writer, introduction to The Decameron, a collection of stories completed c. 1353
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Decameron of Giovanni Boccaccio, trans. John Payne (London: Villon Society, 1886), First Day, introduction. Project Gutenberg eBook #23700.
stimulusBlocks.note: Bracketed words are the translator's. Payne's 1886 English imitates older usage.
stimulusBlocks.text: I say, then, that the years [of the era] of the fruitful Incarnation of the Son of God had attained to the number of one thousand three hundred and forty-eight, when into the notable city of Florence, fair over every other of Italy, there came the death-dealing pestilence, which, through the operation of the heavenly bodies or of our own iniquitous dealings, being sent down upon mankind for our correction by the just wrath of God, had some years before appeared in the parts of the East and after having bereft these latter of an innumerable number of inhabitants, extending without cease from one place to another, had now unhappily spread towards the West.

questions.prompt: Boccaccio's explanation of the plague's causes most clearly reflects
choices: his work as a physician who had studied the disease in Egypt
the religious ideas of his time, which he rejected in favor of scientific medicine
his knowledge that fleas on rats carried the disease from Asia
the religious and astrological ideas common among educated Europeans of his time
questions.explanation: He blames “the heavenly bodies” or God's anger, typical explanations before germ theory.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments
First Day, introduction

choiceExplanations: Boccaccio was a writer and scholar, not a physician.
He repeats these explanations; he does not reject them for modern medicine.
The role of fleas and rats was not understood until the 1890s.
He blames “the heavenly bodies” or God's anger, typical explanations before germ theory.
questions.distinguisher: Explanations reflect what people of the time believed and knew.

questions.prompt: The spread Boccaccio describes is best understood in the context of
choices: busy trade links joining Central Asia, the Black Sea, and Italian ports
busy trade links that began only after Mongol armies had reached Italy
Zheng He's voyages, which carried goods and travelers between China and Italy
Portuguese voyages that brought the disease from West Africa

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Genoese and Venetian ships traded at Black Sea ports such as Caffa, which connected Italy to Mongol-ruled routes.

questions.prompt: How did bananas reach East Africa?
choices: Through trans-Saharan caravans carrying them from West Africa
Through Mongol armies that brought them from Central Asia
Through Indian Ocean maritime contacts with Southeast Asia
Through Indian Ocean contacts, but only after Zheng He's voyages
questions.explanation: Bananas originated in Southeast Asia and New Guinea and crossed the Indian Ocean to Africa.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Bananas reached Africa from the east, by sea, not across the Sahara.
Bananas do not come from Central Asia, and Mongol armies did not reach East Africa.
Bananas originated in Southeast Asia and New Guinea and crossed the Indian Ocean to Africa.
The route is correct, but bananas reached Africa many centuries before Zheng He.
questions.distinguisher: Follow the crop's origin and route.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best shows how new crops could affect population?
choices: New crop → higher food supply → widespread abandonment of cities for the countryside
New crop → higher food supply → equal population growth in every region
New crop → lower food supply → migration out of all farming regions
New crop → higher food supply → population growth where land and labor allowed
questions.explanation: More food could support more people, but results depended on local conditions.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Greater food supply tended to support cities, not empty them.
Food supply mattered, but effects varied by region.
New crops usually raised food supply.
More food could support more people, but results depended on local conditions.
questions.distinguisher: A causal chain needs a qualifier about local conditions.

questions.prompt: Which detail in the passage best shows that the plague raised the value of labor?
choices: Farmers and their families died in the fields without help from physicians or servants
Animals wandered the fields without anyone herding them
Servants who cared for the sick were drawn by “high and extravagant wage”
Grain was left in the fields without being harvested
questions.explanation: People willing to work could demand unusually high pay, a sign of labor scarcity.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments
First Day, introduction

choiceExplanations: This shows suffering in the countryside, not wages.
This shows disruption, not the price of labor.
People willing to work could demand unusually high pay, a sign of labor scarcity.
Unharvested grain shows lost production, not higher wages.
questions.distinguisher: Find the detail about pay.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Giovanni Boccaccio, Florentine writer, introduction to The Decameron, completed c. 1353, describing Florence and its countryside during the plague of 1348
stimulusBlocks.citation: The Decameron of Giovanni Boccaccio, trans. John Payne (London: Villon Society, 1886), First Day, introduction. Project Gutenberg eBook #23700.
stimulusBlocks.note: Husbandmen are farmers. Payne's 1886 English imitates older usage.
stimulusBlocks.text:
By reason whereof there remained unto those (and the number of them, both males and females, was incalculable) who fell sick, none other succour than that which they owed either to the charity of friends (and of these there were few) or the greed of servants, who tended them, allured by high and extravagant wage . . . .

throughout the scattered villages and in the fields, the poor and miserable husbandmen and their families, without succour of physician or aid of servitor, died, not like men, but well nigh like beasts, by the ways or in their tillages or about the houses, indifferently by day and night. . . . the oxen, the asses, the sheep, the goats, the swine, the fowls, nay, the very dogs, so faithful to mankind, being driven forth of their own houses, went straying at their pleasure about the fields, where the very corn was abandoned, without being cut, much less gathered in

questions.prompt: The rural scenes in the passage most directly suggest which economic effect of the plague?
choices: Food prices dropped because farms produced record harvests
Agricultural production fell as farmers died or stopped tending crops
Trade between towns and countryside grew stronger than before
Agricultural production fell, so landlords lowered wages for farmworkers
questions.explanation: Unharvested grain and unherded animals point to lost farm production.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments
First Day, introduction

choiceExplanations: The passage describes abandoned crops, not record harvests.
Unharvested grain and unherded animals point to lost farm production.
The passage describes collapse in the countryside, not stronger trade.
Production fell, but labor scarcity tended to push wages up, not down.
questions.distinguisher: Read the scene literally: crops left in the fields.

questions.prompt: Which feature of the source should a historian consider before using it as evidence?
choices: Boccaccio wrote this as the dramatic opening of a book of stories
Boccaccio was a farmer describing only his own village
Boccaccio wrote fiction, so none of his description can be trusted
Boccaccio wrote centuries after the events in a different country
questions.explanation: The introduction frames his storytelling, so a historian weighs literary purpose while noting he lived through the plague in Florence.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: The introduction frames his storytelling, so a historian weighs literary purpose while noting he lived through the plague in Florence.
He was a Florentine writer, and he describes both city and countryside.
The stories are fiction, but his introduction describes events he witnessed and is widely used as evidence.
He wrote within a few years of 1348, in Florence itself.

questions.prompt: Which explanation of the decline of Great Zimbabwe around 1450 is most defensible?
choices: Several factors, possibly including environmental strain and shifting trade
One factor alone: the sudden arrival of the plague from Indian Ocean trading ports
Conquest by Portuguese soldiers who seized the region's gold mines and trade
A Mongol invasion from the north that destroyed the city's stone walls
questions.explanation: Historians point to overused land and resources and changing trade routes, and they avoid single-cause stories.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Historians point to overused land and resources and changing trade routes, and they avoid single-cause stories.
Single-cause explanations are too simple, and plague is not documented there.
The Portuguese arrived after 1498, after the decline began.
The Mongols never reached southern Africa.
questions.distinguisher: Prefer multicausal explanations where evidence is limited.

questions.prompt: How did the effects of new crops compare with the effects of the plague?
choices: Both affected only China, leaving other regions unchanged
Both moved along trade networks, but crops supported growth while plague cut it
Neither depended on trade; both spread through changes in climate alone, without human help
Both moved along trade networks, and both caused populations to increase
questions.explanation: The same connections carried useful crops and deadly disease, with opposite demographic effects.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Both affected many regions, from China to Europe and Africa.
The same connections carried useful crops and deadly disease, with opposite demographic effects.
Both depended heavily on human movement along trade routes.
Both traveled through networks, but the plague sharply reduced populations.
questions.distinguisher: Same networks, opposite effects.

questions.prompt: Which region was among those hit hard by the plague in the 1300s?
choices: The Inca highlands of the central Andes
Australia's southern coastal settlements
Egypt and Syria in the Mamluk Sultanate
The Aztec cities of the Valley of Mexico
questions.explanation: Cairo and Damascus suffered heavy losses as plague spread through the Mediterranean and Middle East.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: The Andes were also outside Afro-Eurasian networks before 1492.
Australia was not connected to Afro-Eurasian trade networks in this period.
Cairo and Damascus suffered heavy losses as plague spread through the Mediterranean and Middle East.
The Americas were not connected to Afro-Eurasian networks before 1492.
questions.distinguisher: Plague followed Afro-Eurasian connections.

questions.prompt: Which claim about connectivity and the environment is most defensible?
choices: Networks spread useful crops, so their environmental effects were entirely positive
Networks had no environmental effects because people traveled too little
Networks caused the same environmental changes everywhere they reached
Networks spread useful crops and deadly disease, with effects that varied by region
questions.explanation: This claim recognizes benefits and harms and qualifies by region.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Crops helped, but plague and deforestation show harmful effects too.
Movement was large enough to carry crops and diseases across continents.
Effects depended on local environments and responses.
This claim recognizes benefits and harms and qualifies by region.
questions.distinguisher: Benefits, harms, and variation.

questions.prompt: Which claim does the passage make about crop diffusion?
choices: New crops had the same effect wherever they were planted
New crops spread only through the policies of the Song state
A crop's effect depended on how farmers adapted it to local conditions
A crop's effect depended mainly on the government that promoted it
questions.explanation: The passage says arrival “did not determine its effect”; local adaptation did.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: The passage says impact “varied widely.”
Bananas spread across the Indian Ocean without Song involvement.
The passage says arrival “did not determine its effect”; local adaptation did.
The Song promoted Champa rice, but the passage stresses farmers and local conditions.
questions.distinguisher: Find the passage's qualification.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing how historians explain crop diffusion, c. 1000–1450
stimulusBlocks.text:
Champa rice, a fast-ripening variety from mainland Southeast Asia, was promoted by the Song government in the early 1000s, and its spread in southern China allowed some farmers to harvest more than once a year. Bananas, first domesticated in Southeast Asia and New Guinea, had spread across the Indian Ocean to Africa well before this period and became staple foods in parts of East Africa.

In both cases historians stress that a crop's arrival did not determine its effect. Farmers had to adapt planting methods, water management, and labor to local conditions, and the crops' impact varied widely from one region to another.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most strengthen the passage's argument?
choices: An account of Zheng He's voyages to East Africa and the gifts he brought back
Records showing Champa rice spread into many different regions of southern China
A complete list of every crop that farmers grew in Song China
Records showing Champa rice yields varied with irrigation and local labor
questions.explanation: Evidence that results depended on local conditions directly supports the passage's claim.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: The voyages are unrelated to the passage's argument about crops.
Spread shows diffusion, but not that effects depended on local adaptation.
A list does not show how adaptation shaped a crop's effect.
Evidence that results depended on local conditions directly supports the passage's claim.
questions.distinguisher: Evidence must support the specific claim, not just the topic.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes change and continuity in Afro-Eurasian environments, c. 1200–1450?
choices: Farming remained the base of most economies, while crops and diseases spread farther
Farming remained the base of most economies, and no new crops spread in this period
Most people moved to cities, ending the importance of farming
Trade replaced agriculture as the main source of food
questions.explanation: Agriculture persisted as the foundation, while connections carried crops and disease more widely.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: Agriculture persisted as the foundation, while connections carried crops and disease more widely.
Farming persisted, but crops such as Champa rice did spread.
Most people remained rural farmers.
Trade moved some food, but most people ate what was grown nearby.
questions.distinguisher: Name what continued and what changed.

questions.prompt: Which thesis best answers: “Evaluate the extent to which the Black Death changed societies in Afro-Eurasia”?
choices: It had little effect, since only a small share of people died
It caused severe losses and shifted labor relations, but effects varied by region
It improved life for everyone by raising wages in all regions
It caused severe losses, so every society collapsed and never recovered
questions.explanation: This thesis takes a position on extent and qualifies it by region.

sourceLocators.locator: Topic 2.6 learning objectives and historical developments

choiceExplanations: In many regions a third or more of the population died.
This thesis takes a position on extent and qualifies it by region.
Some workers gained, but suffering was enormous, and outcomes differed.
Losses were severe, but many societies recovered over time.
questions.distinguisher: Extent questions call for a weighed claim with qualification.
